To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the evacuation of the pneumo-peritoneum into a suction trap, the appropriate use of a suction trap, and the appropriate use of an instrument change tray can decrease the risk of exposure of the surgical staff to aerosolized blood during laparoscopic surgery.
the use of a closed evacuation system for the pneumoperitoneal cavity during laparoscopic surgery reduces the exposure of the operating room staff to aerosolized blood containing HIV.
the evacuation of the pneumopteronium during a laparoscopic procedure releases aerosolized infected blood and peritonea fluid into the operative field.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reduction of HIV transmission during a laparoscopic procedure.
the development of a method to prevent the release of aerosolized HIV infected blood and peritoneum into the operative suite during laparoscopic surgery.
the reduction of HIV transmission during the evacuation of the pneumopertoneum and during instrument changes during laparoscopic surgery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
laparoscopic procedures can be performed safely in patients infected with HIV, provided appropriate precautions are taken.

the laparoscopic procedure does not increase the risk of transmission to surgical team members, but the risk is not zero and the risk can be reduced by the use of a pneumoperitoneum evacuation device and the use of appropriate surgical techniques. (J Gynecol Surg 1992;8: 235-40)
##

laparoscopic procedures in HIV-infected patients are safe for the surgical team, if the following guidelines are followed: (1) The pneumoperitoneum should be evacuated into a closed system; (2) the surgical team should wear masks during the procedure; and (3) the surgical team must be trained in the use of laparoscopy and must be familiar with the potential for HIV transmission.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the laparoscopic procedure is not a risk-free operation for the surgical team.
we have shown a method of reducing HIV exposure during laparoscopy by using a closed system.
the laparoscopic approach is a viable option for the HIV-infected individual, provided that the surgical team is adequately prepared and protected.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the surgical team is exposed to HIV-infected blood when the pneumoperitoneal cavity is evacuated into the open air.
the surgical team should be protected by a closed system evacuation of the pneumopertitoneum and appropriate precautions during the instrument changes.
the pneumoperitoneal evacuation system can reduce the exposure of the operating room personnel to HIV infected blood aerosols.
